title: Does long hair make a yogi?
odia: ନଖ ବାଳ ରଖି ଭାଲୁଏ ଏ କେତେ ଯୋଗୀ ହେଲେଣି?
literal_meaning: By keeping their nails and hair, how many bears have become yogis?
explanation: The question makes an outward resemblance look absurd. A bear has hair and claws, but those features do not make it a yogi. The joke challenges the idea that an appearance can stand in for the practice it is supposed to signify. Applied elsewhere, it can puncture showy signs of expertise without the patient work behind them; that wider application is an editorial reading of the image.
meaning_odia: ଭାଲୁର ବାଳ ଓ ନଖ ଅଛି ବୋଲି ସେ କଣ ଯୋଗୀ ହୋଇଗଲା? ପ୍ରଶ୍ନଟି ହସାଏ, ପୁଣି ବାହାର ଚେହେରା ଦେଖି ନିଷ୍ପତ୍ତି କରିବାକୁ ଅଟକାଏ। ଯେଉଁ ସାଧନାର ପରିଚୟ ବୋଲି କୌଣସି ଚିହ୍ନକୁ ଧରାଯାଏ, କେବଳ ସେହି ଚିହ୍ନ ରଖିଲେ ସାଧନା ହୋଇଯାଏ ନାହିଁ। ଦକ୍ଷତାର ଦେଖାଣି ଅଛି, ହେଲେ ତାହା ପଛରେ ଅଭ୍ୟାସ ନାହିଁ—ଏପରି ଅବସ୍ଥାକୁ ମଧ୍ୟ ଏହି ଛବି ସହ ତୁଳନା କରାଯାଇପାରେ।
english_summary: Outward resemblance cannot replace the practice it appears to represent.
odia_summary: ବାହାର ଚିହ୍ନ ରଖିଲେ ତାହା ପଛର ସାଧନା ଆସିଯାଏ ନାହିଁ।
usage_example: Someone buys an impressive set of painting tools but never practises; a friend jokes that owning the outward signs does not yet make an artist. (Original imagined example, not collected testimony.)
cultural_context: The source places the question under letting nails and hair grow and explicitly labels it Dhaga. The broader expertise example is an original analogy, not a documented customary use. Do not treat hair, dress or religious affiliation as evidence of dishonesty, or attribute the saying to a particular yogic tradition.
